 Automatic revalidation allows certain travelers to return with an expired visa after a brief trip to Canada or Mexico, if they meet the requirements.

 Translated and edited by   El Cronista EN Published on November 17, 2026 1:41 PM abre en nueva pestaña abre en nueva pestaña abre en nueva pestaña abre en nueva pestaña En esta noticia Who can qualify for automatic revalidation 
 What situations prevent use of this exception 
 Having an expired U.S. visa does not prevent reentry in certain cases. The State Department offers automatic revalidation for certain temporary visitors who take trips of 30 days or less to Canada or Mexico and maintain a valid period of authorized stay.
 The official guide makes clear that this exception is limited in scope and requires meeting other conditions. Final admission decisions rest with Customs and Border Protection (CBP) at the port of entry.

 This option is available to certain holders of expired nonimmigrant visas . They must have a valid admission stamp or Form I-94, endorsed by the Department of Homeland Security.
 Automatic revalidation is not the same as applying for a new visa. It allows reentry to be considered under this exception, as long as the traveler meets the applicable conditions noted above.
 In addition to Canada and Mexico, for F and J categories the guide covers certain adjacent islands . That option does not include travel to Cuba.
 For those holding an M student visa , the destinations covered are limited to Canada and Mexico. The maximum length of absence is 30 days .
 Immigration Laws . Visitor visas can be revoked for studying in the U.S. for anything other than recreation, according to the State Department abre en nueva pestaña What situations prevent use of this exception
 This exception cannot be used by people who applied for a new visa and are waiting for it to be issued, or by those who were denied.
 It also does not apply to those who stayed outside the United States for more than 30 days or traveled to destinations not covered . There are also nationality-based exclusions tied to the designation of state sponsors of terrorism.
